4. Discussion

4.1. Uptake and regeneration of NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) and associated DON release in open ocean and upwelling areas

It is generally assumed that primary production in upwelling systems is mainly supported by NO\(_3^-\) (‘new nitrogen’), which is brought to the surface through the advection of nutrient-rich deep waters to shallower coastal areas. Instead, productivity in open ocean oligotrophic ecosystems is thought to rely on NH\(_4^+\) (‘regenerated nitrogen’) due to the year-round persistence of a strong thermocline that prevents nutrient-rich deep waters to reach the photic layer (Dugdale and Goering, 1967). The \( f\)-ratio quantifies the contribution of Pnew to total production (Pnew+Preg) (Eppley and Peterson, 1979).

Upwelling systems are expected to have high \( f\)-ratios, while oligotrophic systems usually present low \( f\)-ratios. Nevertheless, the recent inclusion of N\(_2\) fixation, NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\) regeneration and DON release rates in the computation of \( f\)-ratios has shown that Pnew is generally overestimated when nitrification is not taken into account, while Preg is generally underestimated when NH\(_4^+\) regeneration is not taken into account (e.g. Fernández and Raimbault, 2007), while gross NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates are underestimated if the associated DON released is not accounted for (e.g. Bronk et al., 1994). In this study, all the above-mentioned fluxes have been included in the calculation of Pnew, Preg and \( f\)-ratios, enhancing the robustness of our results.

The NO\(_3^-\) uptake rates in the upwelling-affected zone were in the range of those observed in the upwelling systems off California (0.10–0.55 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\); Dugdale et al., 2006), and off Peru (0.11–0.14 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\); Blasco et al., 1984), although more recently, rates one to two orders of magnitude lower (0.003–0.02 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)) have been reported for the Peruvian and Chilean upwelling systems (Raimbault and Garcia, 2008; Fernández et al., 2009). While these authors observed considerably high NO\(_3^-\) regeneration (nitrification) rates in the surface waters of the South Pacific Ocean upwelling systems (0.125–1.0 \( \times \) 10\(^{-3}\) \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)), this flux was not detectable during our study in the coastal upwelling off Cape Ghir. In the non-upwelling affected zone (CAIBOX), NO\(_3^-\) uptake and regeneration rates were similar to that observed in a study in the same longitudinal range, but slightly to the north (between ~38 and 45°N) by Fernández and Raimbault (2007), but one to two orders of magnitude higher than previously observed off the coast of Portugal in an area included in our CAIBOX (Slawyk et al., 1997).

Generally, we observed that our NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates were considerably higher than reported in other studies. For example, Fernández et al. (2009) measured NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates ranging from 0.59 \( \times \) 10\(^{-3}\) to 0.006 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) off the Peruvian upwelling system, and Raimbault and Garcia (2008) measured a maximum of 0.02 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) off the Chilean upwelling system. In an open ocean area of the North Atlantic, Fernández and Raimbault (2007) measured NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates up to ~0.01 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\). All these rates are two to three orders of magnitude lower than our NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates measured in the upwelling-affected and non-upwelling-affected areas (Table 3). However, it should be noted that the standard deviation values of our NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates were considerably high (Table 3), and that non-detectable NH\(_4^+\) concentrations where substituted by 5 nM (the detection limit of the method used; Holmes et al., 1999), and therefore those rates can be considered as ‘potential’ NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates (Fernández et al., 2009), potentially overestimating the Preg rates obtained here.

The NH\(_4^+\) regeneration rates measured in this study fall within the range observed in other upwelling and open ocean areas. For example, Fernández et al. (2009) measured NH\(_4^+\) regeneration rates ranging from 0.006 to 0.02 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) off the coast of Peru, and our rates are also in the range of those observed in an upwelling-affected area off the Galician coast (maximum 0.03 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\); Varela et al., 2003). Similarly, the rates of NH\(_4^+\) regeneration observed in the non-upwelling-affected area are in the range of those observed in the North Atlantic by Fernández and Raimbault (2007) (up to ~0.02 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)).

In our study, Preg rates were similar in the upwelling-affected and non-upwelling-affected zones, corroborating the importance of nitrogen regeneration in sustaining primary production (e.g. Fernández and Raimbault, 2007; Clark et al., 2011; Fernández and Farías, 2012). As previously mentioned, open ocean oligotrophic zones are expected to have higher Preg rates than coastal upwelling zones, a pattern typically related to nutrient availability and the related planktonic community structure: picoplankton dominates in oligotrophic areas (e.g. Zubkov et al., 2000), while autotrophic microplankton such as diatoms usually dominate in active upwelling systems (e.g. Hutchings et al., 1995). In contrast, pico- and nanoplanktonic cells predominate the NW Iberian and NW African upwelling systems, whereas diatoms only thrive during upwelling pulses (Espinoza-González et al., 2012; Anabalón et al., unpubl.). In a study performed in the same time of the year, Baltar et al. (2009) found high abundances of heterotrophic prokaryotes (up to 1.5 \( \times \) 10\(^7\) cells mL\(^{-1}\)) in an area where the upwelling filament stretching off Cape Jubi (south of Cape Ghir, off the NW African coast) interacts with the oligotrophic open ocean waters. Similarly, Raimbault and Garcia (2008) observed high NH\(_4^+\) regeneration rates in the upwelling off Chile, associated with the high abundance of heterotrophic plankton. Another piece of evidence is the increasing surface DOC concentrations observed as we move offshore (Table 2), which indicate an enhancement of microbial loop processes, as previously seen in the coastal upwelling zone off Cape Ghir (García-Muñoz et al., 2005).

The DON release rates observed in our study were in the order of those previously measured by Varela et al. (2003) off the Spanish Atlantic coast, but usually an order of magnitude higher than those observed in other oceanic zones (see Table 8.9. in Bronk and Steinberg

(2008)). If we consider gross nitrogen uptake as net nitrogen uptake (nitrogen incorporated into biomass) plus nitrogen ‘lost’ as DON, we can calculate the percentage contribution of DON release to gross nitrogen uptake (Bronk et al., 1994). The percentage contributions of DON release to gross NO3− and gross NH4+ uptake observed (Table 4) were in the range of those previously measured in the Atlantic (Varela et al., 2005). DON release derived from NO3− predominated in non-upwelling-affected zone, while DON released from NH4+ predominated in the upwelling-affected zone (Table 3). This discrepancy between open ocean and coastal zones has been observed in a range of studies (reviewed by Bronk and Steinberg (2008)).

4.2. Distribution of N* and comparison with in situ N2 fixation

The distribution of N* suggests a possible link to in situ N2 fixation in the southern part of the transect, where higher N* values were observed (Fig. 4a), coinciding with the highest N2 fixation rates (see Benavides et al., 2011). However, the high and water column-spread N* values in the northern part of the transect do not correspond with high N2 fixation rates (Fig. 4a; Benavides et al., 2011). Note that the link between the process (N2 fixation) and the signal (high N*) is not direct as there is usually a lag time of several weeks to months between N2 fixation in the epipelagic layer and the N* positive signal indicative of N2 fixation in the mesopelagic layer (Mahaffey et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2013). Moreover, the N* signal travels away from the formation zone along isopycnal surfaces (Mahaffey et al., 2005), which gives room for the possibility that the N* signals observed here had been transported from elsewhere. For example, Palter et al. (2011) suggested that the positive N* signature generated south of the Gulf Stream is transported eastwards through the North Atlantic Current. Alternatively, the positive N* signal may be related to the preferential consumption of phosphorus over nitrogen (see Section 4.3), or to N:P ratios in the dissolved or particulate matter distant from Redfield (Singh et al., 2013).

Singh et al. (2013) recently revisited the distribution of N* over the North Atlantic and the estimated basin-scale yearly N2 fixation rate. They corrected the value of N* considering the local variability of the nitrogen-to-phosphorus (N:P) ratio relative to the Redfield ratio of dissolved nutrients and particulate matter, as well as the deposition of atmospheric nitrogen. These authors argued that N* may have been significantly overestimated in previous publications by considering N:P=16, when it is actually higher, for example, when Trichodesmium is abundant, or when there is an important deposition of high N:P atmospheric materials.

4.3. Contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew and nitrogen excess

The exclusion of N2 fixation rates as a source of Pnew can significantly underestimate the f-ratio (Raimbault and Garcia, 2008). N2 fixation has been estimated to fuel up to 50% of primary production in oligotrophic oceanic areas (Capone et al., 2005). This was not the case in this study, where the contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew was negligible (< 1% in all cases). Similarly, Raimbault and Garcia (2008) did not find a significant contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew in the upwelling system off Chile. Benavides et al. (2011) measured gross and net N2 fixation as derived from the acetylene reduction assay and the uptake of 15N2, respectively. The difference between these two measurements is a good proxy for dissolved nitrogen release (Gallon et al., 2002). In the CAIBEX cruises, an average of ~60% of the N2 fixed was ‘lost’ as dissolved nitrogen (Benavides et al., 2011). Even if a 60% increase is applied to all N2 fixation rates, their contribution to Pnew is still < 1%. Mouriño-Carballido et al. (2011) compared N2 fixation and NO3− diffusion from 16°N to 31°S over central longitudes of the Atlantic. They found that, in the subtropical North Atlantic (~16°N to 9°N), N2 fixation only contributed 2% to Pnew.

N2 fixation rates in our study area are likely affected by wind and coastal upwelling intensity, which are more intense in the summer off NW Iberia, but remain more constant throughout the year off NW Africa (Arístegui et al., 2009). Coastal upwelling provides high NO3− concentrations, which raise Pnew rates (see the average NO3− uptake and Pnew rates for the upwelling-affected area in Table 3). We must note that the measurements presented here correspond to the summer, when the upwelling intensity is maximum off Cape Ghir (Arístegui et al., 2009). Other factor potentially affecting our N2 fixation rates is the deposition of atmospheric dust, brought by the nearby Saharan desert. Saharan dust contains iron and phosphorus, which are thought to be limiting for diazotrophic organisms (Mills et al., 2004). Nevertheless, dust inputs may not raise N2 fixation rates significantly due to (1) a low bioavailability of Fe, for example in the absence of organic ligands-; (2) dust particles sinking out of the photic zone before they can be utilized by diazotrophic organisms (Croot et al., 2004); or (3) a less severe limitation by iron availability. Recently, Luo et al. (2013) gathered all the N2 fixation data available in the literature and conducted statistical analyses to search for connections between the rates and a variety of environmental variables such as temperature, light and iron made available through dust deposition. Their results suggest that, a global scale, iron does not play an important role in shaping the magnitude and distribution of N2 fixation rates. Nevertheless, in general, in situ N2 fixation measurements have shown that rates are boosted when a dust deposition event occurs (e.g. Benavides et al., 2013). Therefore, the role of iron in controlling N2 fixation activity remains unclear and deserves further study. Moreover, it should be noted that the N2 fixation rates presented are likely underestimated according to recent improvements of the 15N2 method. N2 fixation rates measured using 15N2 bubble injections gives rates 50% to 570% times lower than when 15N2 is added dissolved in sample seawater (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012), so a general increase of basin-scale N2 fixation rates in the North Atlantic is expectable when the new method is applied in different locations.

As previously mentioned, Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007) estimated a net nitrogen excess accumulation rate for the area bounded between 25°–42°N and 20°W of 40 ± 22 × 1010 mol N yr−1 or 658 ± 354 μmol N m−2 d−1 with a geochemical box model, which they hypothesized should be due to N2 fixation after discounting other possible sources. This contrasts with the low average N2 fixation rate measured in this study. Considering an average mixed layer depth of 100 m, the resulting volumetric rate of 6.6 ± 3.5 nmol N L−1 d−1 estimated from Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007) is still three orders of magnitude higher the average rate measured experimentally in the same area (1.3 × 10−3 nmol N L−1 d−1; Benavides et al., 2011). If the average N2 fixation rate for the CAIBOX area was 50% higher, the resulting average N2 fixation rate of 2.4 × 10−3 nmol N L−1 d−1 would be still three orders of magnitude lower than estimated by Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007). Even if the highest increment observed between methods is applied (570% by Großkopf et al. (2012)), the nitrogen excess rate observed would still be two orders of magnitude higher. Nevertheless, we must note that surface N2 fixation rates are not necessarily representative of the whole water column. For example, the widespread unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria of group A (UCYN-A) are known to inhabit deeper layers of the world oceans (Moisander et al., 2010), and are the most abundant oceanic diazotrophs (Luo et al., 2012). Moreover, non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs such as α- or β-proteobacteria and Archaea also fix N2 in deeper layers (Riemann et al., 2010). However, deep profiles of N2 fixation rates in this area of the North Atlantic are not available in the literature to date. In summary, a better assessment of depth-integrated N2 fixation rates in this area are needed in order to estimate its true contribution to Pnew.

4.4. Other sources of excess nitrogen accumulation in the water column

Nitrogen anomalies are caused by processes that happen in proportions different from the Redfield N:P ratio, that is, processes that selectively accumulate nitrogen or selectively consume phosphorus (Landolfi et al., 2008). The uptake and regeneration of NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) are expected to occur in proportions according to the Redfield ratio; therefore, the nitrogen excess computed by Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007) in our study area must be caused by other processes. Besides N\(_2\) fixation, Landolfi et al. (2008) considered the following reasons behind nitrogen anomalies: (1) deposition of atmospheric combined nitrogen, which usually has high N:P ratios (Chen et al., 2007; Baker and Croot, 2010; Kanakidou et al., 2012); (2) advection and subsequent remineralization of phosphorus-depleted DOM (Hopkinson and Vallino 2005; Mather et al., 2008); and (3) preferential uptake and/or remineralization of phosphorus over nitrogen (Clark et al., 1998). Below, we include a brief discussion of the role of each of these possibilities in the CAIBOX area (non-upwelling-affected stations, Fig. 1a). Nitrogen excess estimations are not available for the upwelling-affected area (Cape Ghir, Fig. 1b), and therefore will not be further discussed here.

(1) The contribution of atmospheric combined nitrogen deposition to the nitrogen anomaly in the North Atlantic has been previously argued (e.g. Landolfi et al., 2008; Zamora et al., 2010). However, as discussed in Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007), present modeled rates of atmospheric combined nitrogen deposition to the North Atlantic (compiled in Table 5) do not explain the nitrogen excess observed in the CAIBOX area.
(2) A second factor behind nitrogen anomalies would be the injection of dissolved organic matter (DOM) with an N:P ratio > 16 into the mesopelagic layer before it is fully remineralized (Mahaffey et al., 2005; Hansell et al., 2007). It is important to note that the CAIBOX area is bounded to the east by the coastal upwelling system of Iberia – NW Africa. In this sense, García-Muñoz et al. (2005), observed that ~60% of the net primary production near Cape Ghir (~30–31°N) was exported as DOM via upwelling filaments. These are recurrent features of the Iberian-NW African upwelling system and may extend hundreds of kilometers offshore, impacting the thermocline of the North Atlantic subtropical gyre (Álvarez-Salgado et al., 2007). In addition, the release of DON derived from NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) uptake represented considerable percentages of gross uptake (Table 4). This suggests that, adding to atmospheric combined nitrogen deposition, DON advected from the coastal upwelling, and DON produced in situ through NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) uptake may contribute substantially to the observed nitrogen excess in this area.
(3) In contrast with the DON pool, which contains semilabile and refractory fractions (Bronk et al., 2007), the dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) pool is mostly biologically available thanks to the widespread alkaline phosphatase enzyme (Dyhrman et al., 2007). Low inorganic phosphorus availability in the North Atlantic triggers the uptake of DOP, which is selectively remineralized over DON (Kolowith et al., 2001). The preferential remineralization of phosphorus over nitrogen should be assessed by the observation of profiles of DON:DOP ratios (Clark et al., 1998), but unfortunately, DOP data are not available for this study.

A B S T R A C T

We used ¹⁵N-labeled substrates to measure dinitrogen (N₂) fixation, nitrate (NO₃⁻) and ammonium (NH₄⁺) uptake, regeneration and associated dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) release in a coastal upwelling system (Cape Ghir, ~31°N) and an open ocean grid (bounded between 25°–42°N and 20°W) in the Canary Current region during the summer of 2009. New production (Pnew=NO₃⁻ uptake+N₂ fixation+DON released from NO₃⁻ uptake–NO₃⁻ regeneration) was higher in the upwelling than in the open ocean zone (0.126 and 0.014 μmol N L⁻¹ h⁻¹, respectively), while regenerated production (Preg=NH₄⁺ uptake+DON released from NH₄⁺ uptake+NH₄⁺ regeneration) was similar in both zones (0.157 and 0.133 μmol N L⁻¹ h⁻¹, respectively). The resulting f-ratio (Pnew/Pnew+Preg) for the open ocean and upwelling zones was 0.08 and 0.48, respectively. The availability of nitrogen in excess of that expected from Redfield stoichiometry is generally attributed to N₂ fixation. A previous study indicated that our open ocean grid zone had an excess nitrogen production rate of 40 ± 22 × 10¹⁰ mol N yr⁻¹. We revisited this budget including new dissolved organic matter and NO₃⁻ fluxes through the Strait of Gibraltar and estimated a revised nitrogen excess rate of 22 ± 19 × 10¹⁰ mol N yr⁻¹. The average volumetric rate of N₂ fixation for this zone was only 1.3 × 10⁻³ nmol N L⁻¹ d⁻¹, indicating that its influence in Pnew and nitrogen excess production in this part of the Atlantic is negligible.

1. Introduction

One of the greatest current challenges for oceanographers is to balance the oceanic nitrogen budget. At present, it is estimated that nitrogen losses exceed global nitrogen fixation in the upper water column by ~14 × 10¹² mol N yr⁻¹ (Codispoti, 2007). Massive combined nitrogen losses through denitrification and anammox in sediments and oxygen minimum zones of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean push the global budget towards net loss (Deutsch et al., 2001), although the opposite may be found in other basins. In the North Atlantic Ocean, where pelagic denitrification is thought to be negligible (Hansell et al., 2007), excess fixed nitrogen – calculated under the assumption of a nitrogen to phosphorus (N:P) molar ratio of 16 (Redfield, 1934) – has been repeatedly observed with varying rates: 0.15–0.46 × 10¹² mol N yr⁻¹, 0.8 × 10¹² mol N yr⁻¹, 2 × 10¹² mol N yr⁻¹, and 2–9 × 10¹² mol N yr⁻¹ by Hansell et al. (2004, 2007), Gruber and Sarmiento (1997), and Capone et al. (2005).

Dinitrogen (N₂) fixation is a biologically mediated process that reduces N₂ to ammonia via the nitrogenase enzyme complex, carried by several species of cyanobacteria, bacteria and some Archaea (Riemann et al., 2010). N₂ fixation uses phosphate (HPO₄²⁻) but not combined inorganic nitrogen, leaving a signal of excess nitrogen mineralization compared with the expected N:P ratio of 16 in the 70–700 m layer of the North Atlantic Ocean (Mahaffey et al., 2005). This excess nitrogen accumulation is commonly traced by the N* parameter, following the general formulation \( N* = [NO_3^-] - 16 \times [HPO_4^{2-}] \), where [NO₃⁻] and [HPO₄²⁻] are the concentrations of nitrate and HPO₄²⁻, respectively. This equation has been amended by adding constants that bring the global N:P ratio to 16 and the intercept to zero (Gruber and Sarmiento, 1997; Hansell et al., 2004, 2007). (2008)). If we consider gross nitrogen uptake as net nitrogen uptake (nitrogen incorporated into biomass) plus nitrogen ‘lost’ as DON, we can calculate the percentage contribution of DON release to gross nitrogen uptake (Bronk et al., 1994). The percentage contributions of DON release to gross NO3− and gross NH4+ uptake observed (Table 4) were in the range of those previously measured in the Atlantic (Varela et al., 2005). DON release derived from NO3− predominated in non-upwelling-affected zone, while DON released from NH4+ predominated in the upwelling-affected zone (Table 3). This discrepancy between open ocean and coastal zones has been observed in a range of studies (reviewed by Bronk and Steinberg (2008)).

4.2. Distribution of N* and comparison with in situ N2 fixation

The distribution of N* suggests a possible link to in situ N2 fixation in the southern part of the transect, where higher N* values were observed (Fig. 4a), coinciding with the highest N2 fixation rates (see Benavides et al., 2011). However, the high and water column-spread N* values in the northern part of the transect do not correspond with high N2 fixation rates (Fig. 4a; Benavides et al., 2011). Note that the link between the process (N2 fixation) and the signal (high N*) is not direct as there is usually a lag time of several weeks to months between N2 fixation in the epipelagic layer and the N* positive signal indicative of N2 fixation in the mesopelagic layer (Mahaffey et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2013). Moreover, the N* signal travels away from the formation zone along isopycnal surfaces (Mahaffey et al., 2005), which gives room for the possibility that the N* signals observed here had been transported from elsewhere. For example, Palter et al. (2011) suggested that the positive N* signature generated south of the Gulf Stream is transported eastwards through the North Atlantic Current. Alternatively, the positive N* signal may be related to the preferential consumption of phosphorus over nitrogen (see Section 4.3), or to N:P ratios in the dissolved or particulate matter distant from Redfield (Singh et al., 2013).

Singh et al. (2013) recently revisited the distribution of N* over the North Atlantic and the estimated basin-scale yearly N2 fixation rate. They corrected the value of N* considering the local variability of the nitrogen-to-phosphorus (N:P) ratio relative to the Redfield ratio of dissolved nutrients and particulate matter, as well as the deposition of atmospheric nitrogen. These authors argued that N* may have been significantly overestimated in previous publications by considering N:P=16, when it is actually higher, for example, when Trichodesmium is abundant, or when there is an important deposition of high N:P atmospheric materials.

4.3. Contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew and nitrogen excess

The exclusion of N2 fixation rates as a source of Pnew can significantly underestimate the f-ratio (Raimbault and Garcia, 2008). N2 fixation has been estimated to fuel up to 50% of primary production in oligotrophic oceanic areas (Capone et al., 2005). This was not the case in this study, where the contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew was negligible (< 1% in all cases). Similarly, Raimbault and Garcia (2008) did not find a significant contribution of N2 fixation to Pnew in the upwelling system off Chile. Benavides et al. (2011) measured gross and net N2 fixation as derived from the acetylene reduction assay and the uptake of 15N2, respectively. The difference between these two measurements is a good proxy for dissolved nitrogen release (Gallon et al., 2002). In the CAIBEX cruises, an average of ~60% of the N2 fixed was ‘lost’ as dissolved nitrogen (Benavides et al., 2011). Even if a 60% increase is applied to all N2 fixation rates, their contribution to Pnew is still < 1%. Mouriño-Carballido et al. (2011) compared N2 fixation and NO3− diffusion from 16°N to 31°S over central longitudes of the Atlantic. They found that, in the subtropical North Atlantic (~16°N to 9°N), N2 fixation only contributed 2% to Pnew.

N2 fixation rates in our study area are likely affected by wind and coastal upwelling intensity, which are more intense in the summer off NW Iberia, but remain more constant throughout the year off NW Africa (Arístegui et al., 2009). Coastal upwelling provides high NO3− concentrations, which raise Pnew rates (see the average NO3− uptake and Pnew rates for the upwelling-affected area in Table 3). We must note that the measurements presented here correspond to the summer, when the upwelling intensity is maximum off Cape Ghir (Arístegui et al., 2009). Other factor potentially affecting our N2 fixation rates is the deposition of atmospheric dust, brought by the nearby Saharan desert. Saharan dust contains iron and phosphorus, which are thought to be limiting for diazotrophic organisms (Mills et al., 2004). Nevertheless, dust inputs may not raise N2 fixation rates significantly due to (1) a low bioavailability of Fe, for example in the absence of organic ligands-; (2) dust particles sinking out of the photic zone before they can be utilized by diazotrophic organisms (Croot et al., 2004); or (3) a less severe limitation by iron availability. Recently, Luo et al. (2013) gathered all the N2 fixation data available in the literature and conducted statistical analyses to search for connections between the rates and a variety of environmental variables such as temperature, light and iron made available through dust deposition. Their results suggest that, a global scale, iron does not play an important role in shaping the magnitude and distribution of N2 fixation rates. Nevertheless, in general, in situ N2 fixation measurements have shown that rates are boosted when a dust deposition event occurs (e.g. Benavides et al., 2013). Therefore, the role of iron in controlling N2 fixation activity remains unclear and deserves further study. Moreover, it should be noted that the N2 fixation rates presented are likely underestimated according to recent improvements of the 15N2 method. N2 fixation rates measured using 15N2 bubble injections gives rates 50% to 570% times lower than when 15N2 is added dissolved in sample seawater (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012), so a general increase of basin-scale N2 fixation rates in the North Atlantic is expectable when the new method is applied in different locations.

As previously mentioned, Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007) estimated a net nitrogen excess accumulation rate for the area bounded between 25°–42°N and 20°W of 40 ± 22 × 1010 mol N yr−1 or 658 ± 354 μmol N m−2 d−1 with a geochemical box model, which they hypothesized should be due to N2 fixation after discounting other possible sources. This contrasts with the low average N2 fixation rate measured in this study. Considering an average mixed layer depth of 100 m, the resulting volumetric rate of 6.6 ± 3.5 nmol N L−1 d−1 estimated from Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007) is still three orders of magnitude higher the average rate measured experimentally in the same area (1.3 × 10−3 nmol N L−1 d−1; Benavides et al., 2011). If the average N2 fixation rate for the CAIBOX area was 50% higher, the resulting average N2 fixation rate of 2.4 × 10−3 nmol N L−1 d−1 would be still three orders of magnitude lower than estimated by Álvarez and Álvarez-Salgado (2007). Even if the highest increment observed between methods is applied (570% by Großkopf et al. (2012)), the nitrogen excess rate observed would still be two orders of magnitude higher. Nevertheless, we must note that surface N2 fixation rates are not necessarily representative of the whole water column. For example, the widespread unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria of group A (UCYN-A) are known to inhabit deeper layers of the world oceans (Moisander et al., 2010), and are the most abundant oceanic diazotrophs (Luo et al., 2012). Moreover, non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs such as α- or β-proteobacteria and Archaea also fix N2 in deeper layers (Riemann et al., 2010). However, deep profiles of N2 fixation rates in this area of the North Atlantic are not available in the literature to date. In summary, a better assessment of depth-integrated N2 fixation rates in this area are needed in order to estimate its true contribution to Pnew.

Diazotroph community structure and the role of nitrogen fixation in the nitrogen cycle in the Chukchi Sea (western Arctic Ocean)

Takuhei Shiozaki 1,2*, Amane Fujiwara, 3 Minoru Ijichi, 1 Naomi Harada, 2 Shigeto Nishino, 3 Shinro Nishi, 4 Toshi Nagata, 1 Koji Hamasaki 1
1Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa, Chiba, Japan
2Research and Development Center for Global Change, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, Yokosuka, Kanagawa, Japan
3Institute of Arctic Climate and Environment Research, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, Yokosuka, Kanagawa, Japan
4Research and Development Center for Marine Biosciences, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, Yokosuka, Kanagawa, Japan

Abstract
Marine nitrogen fixation occurs not only in subtropical and tropical regions but also in colder regions. However, the distribution of diazotrophs, nitrogen fixation rate, and its contribution to the nitrogen cycle in the Arctic Ocean remain poorly understood. We examined the diazotroph community structure and activity in the shelf and off-shelf regions of the Chukchi Sea, western Arctic Ocean, during late summer 2015. The nitrate and ammonium assimilation rates were determined simultaneously to gain insights into the role of nitrogen fixation in the nitrogen cycle of the region. The diazotroph community determined by Illumina sequencing was mainly composed of Cluster III nifH phylotypes (putative anaerobes), accounting for > 80% of the total sequences examined, except for one surface sample. This result is strikingly different from previous findings in other oceanic regions. The nifH sequences other than those from Cluster III were mostly affiliated with UCYN-A2 (symbiotic cyanobacteria), which accounted for < 15% of the total sequences. UCYN-A2 tended to be abundant (maximum 2.9 × 10^3 copies L^{-1}) in the high-temperature low-salinity water mass that is characteristic of Pacific-originating water. Nitrogen fixation rate was detectable at most stations, with a range of 0.08–3.60 nmol L^{-1} d^{-1}, displaying no clear relationship with depth (light intensity) or nitrate or ammonium concentration. Nitrogen fixation locally exceeded nitrate assimilation, but accounted for 1.00% at most in the total nitrogen assimilation in the euphotic zone.

Biological nitrogen fixation, which is the reduction of atmospheric N_2 to ammonia by diazotrophic microbes, is a major source of oceanic-fixed nitrogen, which supports new production (Karl et al. 1997; Shiozaki et al. 2009, 2017) and is eventually lost from marine ecosystems through denitrification (Gruber 2008). Geochemical estimates have indicated that the nitrogen gain by nitrogen fixation and the loss by denitrification were roughly in balance during the Holocene (Brandes and Devol 2002; Deutsch et al. 2004). However, rate measurement data have shown that denitrification far exceeds nitrogen fixation in the ocean, raising the possibility that the marine nitrogen fixation rate may be largely underestimated (Codispoti 2007).

In recent decades, marine diazotrophs and their activities have been extensively studied in tropical and subtropical regions (Sohm et al. 2011; Luo et al. 2012) where chronic dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) depletion favors diazotrophic nitrogen acquisition, which imparts a higher energetic cost than the uptake of DIN (Falkowski 1983). However, recent studies have increasingly found that nitrogen fixation proceeds at a measurable rate in higher latitude regions, including in DIN-rich (> 1 \( \mu \)mol L^{-1}) waters (Blais et al. 2012; Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015; Shiozaki et al. 2015a). These results suggest that the area of the world oceans where nitrogen fixation occurs is much larger than previously thought.

</page>

<page number="1">

Fig. 1. Sampling stations in the Chukchi Sea during the MR15-03 cruise. Red and white names indicate stations in the shelf and off-shelf regions, respectively. Colors in each plot correspond to the freshwater fraction: left and right semicircles denote the fraction of sea ice meltwater (\( f_{SIM} \)) and other fresh water (\( f_{OF} \)), respectively. Background contours indicate sea ice concentration (SIC) observed by AMSR2 and sea surface temperature (SST) observed by MODIS during the study period.

Limited data have suggested that the nitrogen fixation proceeds in the Arctic Ocean. Blais et al. (2012) found nitrogen fixation rates in the range of 0.02–4.45 nmol N L\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\) in the surface and chlorophyll maximum layers of the Canada Basin. That and other studies have found that *nifH* genes, encoding the iron subunit of nitrogenase, are omnipresent in the Arctic Ocean (Blais et al. 2012; Díez et al. 2012; Fernández-Méndez et al. 2016). Many of these genes were dissimilar to those previously observed from tropical and subtropical oceans, and were likely indigenous to the Arctic environment. However, the available data were based primarily on clone library analyses with limited sequencing depth and did not represent complete coverage of community structure. We know little about the factors controlling diazotrophic activity and the role of nitrogen fixation in nitrogen cycle in the Arctic Ocean.

This study examined the vertical distribution of nitrogen fixation rates in the euphotic zone and diazotroph community structure using a deep sequencing approach in the Chukchi Sea of the western Arctic Ocean (Fig. 1). We also determined the nitrate and ammonium assimilation rates simultaneously to examine the contribution of nitrogen fixation to the nitrogen cycle in the region. The Chukchi Sea overlays a large continental shelf and receives Pacific water through the Bering Strait (Coachman et al. 1975; Walsh et al. 1989; Shimada et al. 2001). The shelf region is very productive and this is sustained by the intrusion of nutrient-rich Anadyr water from the Bering Sea (Walsh 1989), whereas the off-shelf region is generally oligotrophic due to stratification caused by the influence of riverine and sea ice meltwater (Carmack and Wassmann 2006; Nishino et al. 2015). Our sampling was conducted to investigate the broad environmental gradient covering the shelf and off-shelf regions of the Chukchi Sea.

*Samples and methods*

**Water sampling and environmental data**

Samples were obtained from 21 stations while onboard the R/V *Mirai* (MR15-03) in the Chukchi Sea from 06 September 2015 to 03 October 2015 (Fig. 1). The light intensity depth profiles were determined just before sampling using a PRR-800

</page>

<page number="2">

spectroradiometer (Biospherical Instruments, San Diego, California, U.S.A.). Samples for incubation experiments and DNA were collected from depths corresponding to 100%, 10%, 1%, and 0.1% of surface light intensity. In addition to those light depths, samples for nutrients (\( n = 2 \)) and chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \); \( n = 1 \)) determinations were collected at some depths within the upper 100 m. Surface samples were collected using a bucket (100% light depth), and the subsurface layer samples were collected with a Niskin-X bottle. Temperature, salinity, and DO profiles were measured using a SBE 911 plus CTD system (Sea-Bird Electronics, Bellevue, Washington, U.S.A.). The oxygen and salinity sensors were calibrated using bottle data taken during the entire cruise. The nitrate, nitrite, ammonium, and phosphate concentrations were determined colorimetrically at sea (Hansen and Koroleff 1999) using QuAAtro 2-HR systems (SEAL Analytical, Southampton, UK). The detection limits of nitrate, nitrite, ammonium, and phosphate were 0.05 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\), 0.01 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\), 0.07 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\), and 0.003 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\), respectively. The upper limit of the nitracline was defined as the depth at which the nitrate concentration equaled 1 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\). Samples for Chl \( a \) (290 mL) were filtered onto 25 mm GF/F filters (Whatman, Kent, UK). Chl \( a \) concentrations were measured fluorometrically at sea using a 10-AU fluorometer (Turner Designs, San Jose, California, U.S.A.) after extraction with \( N, N \)-dimethylformamide. The fractions of sea ice meltwater (\( f_{SIM} \)) and other fresh water (\( f_{OF} \)) were calculated from the relationship between total alkalinity and salinity data proposed by Yamamoto-Kawai et al. (2005, 2009). Total alkalinity was determined by potentiometric titration (Yao and Byrne 1998) using a spectrophotometric system (Nippon ANS, Tokyo, Japan) during the cruise.

DNA extraction, sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and qPCR assay

Seawater samples (2 L) for DNA analyses were collected onto Sterivex-GP pressure filter units with a 0.22-\( \mu \)m pore size (Millipore, Billerica, Massachusetts, U.S.A.) and stored at \(-80^{\circ}\)C until onshore analysis. Total DNA was extracted using a ChargeSwitch Forensic DNA Purification Kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, California, U.S.A.), following the manufacturer’s instructions (Shiozaki et al. 2017). The DNA concentration was determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (NanoDrop Technologies, Wilmington, Delaware, U.S.A.). Fragments of the \( nifH \) genes were amplified by nested PCR (Zehr and Turner 2001) as previously described (Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015; Shiozaki et al. 2017), with some modifications. The samples were selected from stations at which the nitrogen fixation rate was detected. The vertical diazotroph community structure was examined from the surface to the 0.1% light depth at stations (Sta.) 13 and 108 where vertical mixing was strong in the shelf region. Additionally, the sample at the 0.1% light depth at Sta. 6, where nitrogen fixation occurred even in extremely high nitrate concentration (19.9 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\)), was examined. In the off-shelf region, the vertical diazotroph community structure was determined at randomly selected Sta. 56 and 62, and surface communities were examined at Sta. 39, 54, and 94. In the first-round PCR, DNA samples were added to Tks Gflex DNA Polymerase Low DNA (Takara Bio, Shiga, Japan) with the nifH3 and nifH4 primers (Zehr and Turner 2001). The forward and reverse primers (nifH1 and nifH2 primers) (Zehr and Turner 2001) with attached Illumina adapters Rd1SP (5'-ACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT-3') and Rd2SP (5'-GTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTTCTTCCGATCT-3'), respectively, were added to amplicons for the second-round PCR, which was performed in triplicate for each sample. The first and second PCR rounds were 30 cycles each. The triplicate PCR products were pooled and purified using the AMPure XP purification kit (Beckman Coulter, Brea, California, U.S.A.). Then, index PCR was performed to attach the 7-base barcode (Supporting Information Table S1) using KAPA HiFi HotStart Ready Mix (KAPA Biosystems, Boston, Massachusetts, U.S.A.), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The PCR products were purified again using the AMPure XP purification kit and were quantified with a Quantus Fluorometer (Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, U.S.A.). All samples were finally pooled at an equimolar concentration and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, California, U.S.A.), wherein 300 bp fragments from each end of the libraries were sequenced using the MiSeq reagent kit v3 (600 cycles; Illumina) with Phix control v3 (Illumina).

Sequencing reads were demultiplexed using the standard Illumina pipeline. Primer sequences were trimmed from the sequence using cutadapt (Martin 2011). Then, the paired-end reads were merged using PEAR (Zhang et al. 2014). Subsequent analyses were performed in Claident v.0.2.2016.07.05 (Tanabe and Toju 2013). The merged sequences were trimmed with a minimum quality value of 30 and a minimum sequence length of 300 bp. Sequence errors were further removed by clustering analysis implemented in Claident. Chimeras were removed using UCHIME (Edgar et al. 2011). Operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were grouped at 97% nucleotide similarity by clclassseqv in Claident. The OTU sequences were translated into amino acid sequences, analyzed using BLAST searches against the National Center for Biotechnology Information databases, and non-\( nifH \) OTUs or OTUs with a frame shift were removed. The \( nifH \) sequences were aligned with MUSCLE in the MEGA6 package (Tamura et al. 2013). A phylogenetic tree was constructed using the maximum likelihood method, and bootstrap values were determined using 1000 iterations implemented in MEGA6. The recovered sequences have been deposited in the DNA Data Bank of Japan Sequence Read Archive under accession number DRA005723. Nonmetric multidimensional scaling was carried out with a Bray–Curtis distance matrix to examine the changes in gene biodiversity using PRIMER 6 software.

Nitrogen fixation
Samples for nitrogen fixation were collected in duplicate acid-cleaned 1.2 L polycarbonate bottles. Nitrogen fixation was determined using the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas dissolution method (Mohr et al. 2010). Samples (1.2 L) collected for determining the initial \( ^{15} \)N enrichment of particulate organic matter were filtered immediately at the beginning of incubation (\( n = 1 \)). \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\)-enriched filtered seawater (50 mL) was injected, and the bottles were sealed with a thermoplastic elastomer cap. \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas was dissolved at a ratio of 10 mL \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) per 1 L seawater. The volume of dissolved N\(_2\) was calculated using the equation given by Weiss (1970), and we assumed that added \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) was completely dissolved. The resulting N\(_2\) substrate enrichment at the beginning of incubation was approximately 3–4% (Supporting Information Table S3). A recent study showed that commercial \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas could be contaminated by \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate and ammonium (Dabundo et al. 2014). Dabundo et al. (2014) suggested that the contamination may occur during the production process of the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas, and it differed among different batches, even for those from the same distributor, although they did not examine the product of SI Science (Yokohama, Japan). The SI Science \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas is produced by the oxidation of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium sulfate by potassium hypobromite (Nakane 1963), followed by purification using a molecular sieve and liquid nitrogen. Shiozaki et al. (2015b) examined the contamination of nitrate and ammonium for two different batches of the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas stock purchased from SI Science and found that the contamination was negligible (< nmol L\(^{-1}\)) for all batches examined. Furthermore, they reported that the contamination of nitrate and ammonium in a \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) dissolved water (10 mL \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) per 1 L seawater) was undetectable (< nmol L\(^{-1}\) level). In the present study, we added 50 mL of \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) dissolved water to the samples. Therefore, \( ^{15} \)N-labeled substrates in the samples were below 5 \( \times \) 10\(^{-2}\) nmol N L\(^{-1}\). When the substrate concentration in the seawater was 0.05 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) (the detection limit of our analysis), the concentration of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled substrate would be < 1/1000 lower than that of seawater. In this case, the \( ^{15} \)N concentration would be too low to detect the uptake rate (Shiozaki et al. 2009). Therefore, we believe that our estimates of the N\(_2\)-fixation rate were affected little by impurities in the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas. The bottles were incubated in an on-deck incubator filled with flowing surface seawater for 24 h. Incubations were terminated by gentle filtration onto pre-combusted (450°C for 6 h) GF/F filters (Whatman). The filters were kept frozen before onshore analysis. The filters were dried at 50°C overnight, and then exposed to HCl fumes for 2 h. Total nitrogen and isotope ratios were determined using a DELTA V advantage mass spectrometer (Thermo Electron, Waltham, Massachusetts, U.S.A.) connected to a Flash EA elemental analyzer (Thermo Electron). The nitrogen fixation rate was calculated using the equation proposed by Montoya et al. (1996). We performed a sensitivity analysis for the nitrogen fixation measurements to determine quantifiable nitrogen fixation rates (Montoya et al. 1996; Gradoville et al. 2017). The minimum quantifiable rate for each sample was calculated using standard propagation of errors based on the observed variability between replicate samples, and ranged from 0.05 nmol N L\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\) to 3.30 nmol N L\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Supporting Information Table S3).

Nitrate and ammonium assimilation
Samples for nitrate assimilation were collected at all stations, and those for ammonium assimilation were collected at Sta. 32, 39, 47, 53, 54, 55, 56, 62, 68, 75, 82, 85, 94, 98, and 108. These samples were collected in acid-cleaned 1.2-L polycarbonate bottles during the daytime. Samples were also collected for nighttime incubation of ammonium assimilation. For nighttime incubation, the bottles were incubated without \( ^{15} \)N tracer in an on-deck incubator until midnight, and then \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium was added. For daytime incubation, \( ^{15} \)N tracer was added immediately after water collection. The nitrate and ammonium assimilation rates were determined by the Michaelis–Menten kinetics approach (Shiozaki et al. 2009) using samples obtained from the surface and 10% light depth. \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate (99 atom% \( ^{15} \)N; SI Science) was added at final tracer concentrations of 10 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 20 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 100 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and 2000 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium (99 atom% \( ^{15} \)N; SI Science) was added at final tracer concentrations of 8 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 25 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 125 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and 1250 nmol L\(^{-1}\). The enrichment of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate and ammonium in samples obtained from the 1% and 0.1% light depths averaged 23.3% ± 24.9% and 18.6% ± 13.7%, respectively, which was higher than the tracer level (< 10%). Therefore, nitrate and ammonium assimilation at the 1% and 0.1% light depths might be overestimated. The bottles spiked with \( ^{15} \)N tracer were incubated for < 2 h in the on-deck incubator. Incubations were terminated by gentle filtration onto pre-combusted GF/F filters. The analytical procedure for nitrate and ammonium assimilation was the same as that for nitrogen fixation. Sea surface temperature was lower in the off-shelf region than in the shelf region (Fig. 1 and 2, Supporting Information Fig. S1, Table 1), and relatively warm water (ca. 2–5°C) was observed in the subsurface layer. Surface salinity also tended to decrease from the shelf (27.08–32.8) to the off-shelf region (25.49–30.78) (Table 1). Large fractions of sea ice meltwater (\( f_{SIM} \)) and other fresh water (\( f_{OF} \)) in the off-shelf region (Fig. 1) indicated that the low temperature and salinity at the surface was attributable to sea ice meltwater and riverine input. The heterogeneous distribution of water masses with different \( f_{SIM} \) and \( f_{OF} \) indicated that the water mass structure was complex. The minimum dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration in the study area was 218 \( \mu \)mol kg\(^{-1}\) (Supporting Information Fig. S2), indicating that oxygen was not depleted in the water column.

In surface waters, the nitrate concentrations were low (\( < 0.1 \) \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\)) in the off-shelf region except for Sta. 23 and 82, whereas they were relatively high (0.11–20.1 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\)) in the shelf region. Vertically, nitrate concentrations tended to increase with depth (Fig. 2). The average depth of the nitracline in the off-shelf region (56 ± 12 m) was significantly (\( p < 0.05 \), \( t \)-test) deeper than that in the shelf region (26 ± 8 m). Surface ammonium concentrations were relatively low (\( < 0.07–0.14 \) \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\)) and high (0.08–4.70 \( \mu \)mol N L\(^{-1}\)) in the off-shelf and shelf regions, respectively (Table 1). Ammonium concentrations tended to increase with depth in the shelf region except for Sta. 1 and 108, whereas the vertical distribution of ammonium was complex in the off-shelf region (Fig. 2, Supporting Information Fig. S1). Phosphate concentrations were positively correlated with nitrate concentrations (\( r = 0.966 \); Pearson’s correlation; Supporting Information Table S4). The nitrate + ammonium/phosphate (N/P) ratio of inorganic nutrients ranged from 0.17 to 10.9, much lower than the Redfield ratio (Supporting Information Table S4). The surface Chl a concentrations (0.27–4.28 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\)) were generally higher in the shelf region than in the off-shelf region (Table 1), with the highest value found at Sta. 1 on the shelf. Vertically, the peak Chl a concentrations were generally located near the surface except a peak near the bottom (depth, 50 m) found at Sta. 102 (Supporting Information Fig. S2).

Similar diazotrophic communities were observed in the surface and the 0.1% light depth at both Sta. 13 and 108, where the water column was well mixed vertically (Fig. 4). Otu1, 3, and 4 were commonly observed in these samples. These OTU groups were also retrieved from the 0.1% light depth of Sta. 6 and the 1% light depth of Sta. 56. These samples fell near each other on the nonmetric multidimensional scaling plot (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Otu1 was the most abundant OTU, and exhibited 100% nucleotide sequence similarity to nifH retrieved from sediment in the North Sea (NCBI accession No. KP959477). In contrast, the surface water diazotroph communities at Sta. 39, 54, and 94 in the off-shelf region significantly differed, even though they were only collected a few kilometers away from each other (Fig. 4).

The UCYN-A2 nifH sequence accounted for a maximum of 15% of all nifH sequences (surface water at Sta. 54); thus, they were not a dominant diazotroph in the Chukchi Sea. However, UCYN-A2 was extensively detected by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assay (16 of 21 stations) (Fig. 5, Supporting Information Fig. S4). UCYN-A2 was found from the surface to 0.1% light depth, but did not occur below 66 m. Maximum abundance (2.9 × 10^3 copies L^{-1}) was observed at the 10% light depth of Sta. 11. UCYN-A2 tended to be abundant in water masses with higher temperatures (Fig. 6). The minimum temperature for detecting UCYN-A2 was −0.39°C. UCYN-A1 was under the detection limit of the qPCR assay at all stations.

Nitrate assimilation at the 0.1% light depth was higher than in a sample collected just above that depth at most stations (14 of 21). Depth-integrated nitrate assimilation varied in the range of 170–6130 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). The depth integrated nitrogen fixation accounted for up to 17.0% (mean ± standard deviation, 3.59% ± 4.14%) of the sum of nitrate assimilation and nitrogen fixation in the euphotic zone. The contribution was significantly higher in the off-shelf region (5.40% ± 4.66%) than the shelf region (1.18% ± 1.24%) (p < 0.05, t-test). The contribution of nitrogen fixation to the total nitrogen assimilation (the sum of nitrogen fixation, nitrate assimilation, and ammonium assimilation) in the euphotic zone was between 0.08% and 1.00%.

Discussion
Diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea
This study is the first to elucidate the diazotroph community structure in the Arctic Ocean using a deep sequencing approach. Although some studies have examined diazotroph communities in Arctic regions (Blais et al. 2012; Díez et al. 2012; Fernández-Méndez et al. 2016), these studies analyzed clone libraries with a limited number of sequences, being compromised by phylogenetic resolution. A notable finding of the present study is that Cluster III phylotypes dominated the diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea. We found that Cluster III accounted for > 80% of the total nifH sequences examined, except for one surface sample. Cluster III includes putative anaerobes belonging to Bacteria and Archaea (Zehr et al. 2003) and has been reported to be a major constituent of the nifH sequences retrieved from marine and estuarine sediments (Bertics et al. 2013; Newell et al. 2016). Studies have also recovered Cluster III nifH sequences from coastal marine waters (e.g., Moisander et al. 2008; Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015; Shiozaki et al. 2015a). In the Canadian Arctic, Blais et al. (2012) found many nifH sequences affiliated with Cluster III in water samples collected from rivers, estuaries, and fjords. By contrast, in offshore areas of the Arctic Ocean, the retrieved nifH sequences were mainly affiliated with Cluster I phylotypes including cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria (Díez et al. 2012; Fernández-Méndez et al. 2016). Considering this information, we speculate that Cluster III phylotypes in the investigated waters were allochthonous and derived from the coastal region or sediments. In support of this notion, river-derived water (high fOF water) was observed in the off-shelf region stations (Fig. 1),

</page>

<page number="10">

suggesting the influence of the Mackenzie River water (Yamamoto-Kawai et al. 2005), and the most abundant OTU, Otu1 (Fig. 4), was identical (100% similarity) to a sequence previously retrieved from the sediment of the North Sea. In addition to the riverine influence, the wind-induced resuspension of shelf sediments (Uchimiya et al. 2016) and subsequent lateral transport of particles from the shelf to the off-shelf region (Yamada et al. 2015) might also contribute to the spread of sediment-associated microbes in the water column of the investigated region. Further studies are required to verify the model of Cluster III transport in the Chukchi Sea.

We identified cyanobacterial UCYN-A1 and -A2 nifH sequences, and UCYN-A2 was abundant and widely distributed throughout the study area. UCYN-A1 and -A2 are major diazotrophs in the tropical and subtropical oligotrophic oceans (Farnelid et al. 2016). The presence of UCYN-A in the Arctic Ocean was predicted based on 16S rRNA gene sequences (Martínez-Pérez et al. 2016), but has not been quantified. A recent study reported high abundance of UCYN-A2 (1.2 × 10^5 copies L^{-1}) in Alaskan coastal waters of the Bering Sea (Shiozaki et al. 2017). Alaskan coastal water flows into the Chukchi Sea as Pacific-originating water (Coachman et al. 1975; Shimada et al. 2001). A high abundance of UCYN-A2 tended to be observed in the high-temperature low-salinity water mass (Fig. 5b), which is characteristic of Pacific-originating water (Coachman et al. 1975). Thus, UCYN-A2 in the Chukchi Sea is likely delivered there from the Pacific Ocean. The maximum abundance of UCYN-A2 in the Chukchi Sea (2.9 × 10^3 copies L^{-1}) was about 40-fold lower than that in the Bering Sea (Shiozaki et al. 2017). UCYN-A abundance is known to be related to water temperature (Moisander et al. 2010), suggesting that UCYN-A2 abundance decreased with decreasing water temperature during their northward transit from the Bering Sea to the Chukchi Sea.

Nitrogen fixation and its importance in nitrogen cycle in the Chukchi Sea

We found that the vertical distribution pattern of the nitrogen fixation rate was complex, displaying sporadic subsurface peaks. In general, in tropical and subtropical waters, nitrogen fixation is high near the surface and decreases with depth. This can be explained by the prevalence of cyanobacterial diazotrophs that require light as an energy source (Church et al. 2009; Shiozaki et al. 2017). The complex vertical pattern of nitrogen fixation rates observed in this study could be due to the contribution of non-photosynthetic bacteria, whose nitrogen fixation is independent of the light environment, to nitrogen fixation. Interestingly, Cluster III phylotypes were dominant in our study area. As discussed in the previous section, these diazotrophs are putative anaerobes (Zehr et al. 2003) and were conceivably derived from coastal regions or sediments to the oxic water column. Anaerobes can be metabolically active in oxic seawater if they inhabit particles with anoxic microzones (Paerl and Prufert 1987). However, we lack evidence supporting (or refuting) the idea that Cluster III diazotrophs were fixing nitrogen in anoxic microzones. Whether the dominant Cluster III phylotypes contribute significantly to nitrogen fixation in oxic water columns clearly deserves further scrutiny.

Nitrogen fixation is regulated not only by light but also by other factors including iron, phosphorus, and temperature (Sohm et al. 2011 and references therein). The nitrogen fixation rate from the surface to the 0.1% light depth in the Chukchi Sea (0.08–3.60 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}) was higher than that reported in the literature for offshore stations (surface and SCM) in the Canadian sector of the Arctic Ocean (0.01–0.18 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}, Blais et al. 2012) (difference of means, \( p < 0.05 \), \( t \)-test), while it was comparable to that reported for estuarine stations (0.40–3.38 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}, Blais et al. 2012). Blais et al. (2012) suggested that the difference in nitrogen fixation between offshore and estuarine stations was attributable to the dissolved iron concentration. The nitrogen fixation enzyme nitrogenase contains iron in its active site, and thus, diazotrophs require much more iron for growth than other microbes (Kustka et al. 2002). Dissolved iron concentrations in the Chukchi Sea are very high (maximum, 33.1 nM) due to supply from shelf sediments and the Mackenzie River (Cid et al. 2012; Hioki et al. 2014; Kondo et al. 2016). Thus, the iron levels would be sufficient to support diazotrophs in our study area. Meanwhile, these nitrogen fixation rates are lower than those reported in lower latitude coastal environments, where the maximum nitrogen fixation often exceeds 10 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1} (Shiozaki et al. 2010, 2014b). Phosphorus limitation of nitrogen fixation generally occurs in phosphate-depleted waters (Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al. 2001). Phosphate was detected at all of the stations in our study area, and thus, did not appear to limit nitrogen fixation. There is a strong temperature difference between the Arctic and subtropical oceans. However, very high nitrogen fixation (> 60 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}) has been reported in a cold (4.1°C) temperate coastal environments (Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015), suggesting that temperature is not the reason for lower nitrogen fixation in the Chukchi Sea and Canadian Arctic coastal regions. Note that diazotroph community structure in our study area was notably different from that in other regions where Cluster I diazotrophs dominate (Farnelid et al. 2011; Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015), which may be related to the difference of nitrogen fixation activity.

The nitrate and ammonium assimilation rate was higher near the surface and decreased with depth, which is consistent with previous results for the Chukchi Sea (Lee et al. 2007; Nishino et al. 2011). Nitrate and ammonium assimilation integrated to the 0.1% light depth was within the range of previous studies in the Chukchi Sea (0.032–17.1 mmol and 1.02–36.9 N m^{-2} d^{-1}, respectively; Lee et al. 2007; Yun et al. 2014; Shiozaki et al. 2016). Our estimates showed that

</page>

<page number="11">

nitrogen fixation accounts for at most only 1.00% of the total nitrogen assimilation rates (nitrogen fixation + nitrate and ammonium assimilation). In the Arctic Ocean, the assimilation of other forms of nitrogen (urea and amino acid) is reportedly as high as nitrate and ammonium assimilation (Baer et al. 2017). Therefore, nitrogen fixation is a minor process in the overall nitrogen cycle. However, nitrate assimilation in the off-shelf region was significantly lower than on the shelf, and nitrogen fixation in the off-shelf region sometimes exceeded nitrate assimilation and accounted for up to 17.0% of the sum of nitrate assimilation and nitrogen fixation in the euphotic zone, indicating a significant contribution to the local nitrogen cycle. Water stratification in the Arctic Ocean is preceded by ice melt, particularly in the Canada Basin, which includes the off-shelf region of the Chukchi Sea (McLaughlin and Carmack 2010; Nishino et al. 2011). Thus, nitrogen fixation could become more important to the nitrogen cycle of this region in the future.

Conclusions

This study documented that nitrogen fixation occurs throughout the Chukchi Sea, and has a local impact on the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen fixation was not affected by light or nitrate concentration, which could be due to the contribution of non-photosynthetic bacteria. Light-independent nitrogen fixation suggests the occurrence of nitrogen fixation below the euphotic zone and during the winter dark period. To the best of our knowledge, the western Arctic Ocean is the only oceanic region where Cluster III phyotypes dominate the diazotroph community in the euphotic zone. Arctic surface water masses can be broadly divided into waters originating in the Pacific and the Atlantic (Gordienko 1958). This water circulation pattern may differentiate the diazotroph community between the Chukchi Sea and Atlantic Arctic Ocean. We found that UCYN-A1 and -A2 in the Chukchi Sea were delivered from the Pacific Ocean. The Pacific inflow has tended to increase recently, inducing an increase in the heat flux (Woodgate et al. 2012; Itoh et al. 2013). This environmental change may alter the diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea.

In addition to the riverine influence, the wind-induced resuspension of shelf sediments (Uchimiya et al. 2016) and subsequent lateral transport of particles from the shelf to the off-shelf region (Yamada et al. 2015) might also contribute to the spread of sediment-associated microbes in the water column of the investigated region. Further studies are required to verify the model of Cluster III transport in the Chukchi Sea.

We identified cyanobacterial UCYN-A1 and -A2 nifH sequences, and UCYN-A2 was abundant and widely distributed throughout the study area. UCYN-A1 and -A2 are major diazotrophs in the tropical and subtropical oligotrophic oceans (Farnelid et al. 2016). The presence of UCYN-A in the Arctic Ocean was predicted based on 16S rRNA gene sequences (Martínez-Pérez et al. 2016), but has not been quantified. A recent study reported high abundance of UCYN-A2 (1.2 × 10^5 copies L^{-1}) in Alaskan coastal waters of the Bering Sea (Shiozaki et al. 2017). Alaskan coastal water flows into the Chukchi Sea as Pacific-originating water (Coachman et al. 1975; Shimada et al. 2001). A high abundance of UCYN-A2 tended to be observed in the high-temperature low-salinity water mass (Fig. 5b), which is characteristic of Pacific-originating water (Coachman et al. 1975). Thus, UCYN-A2 in the Chukchi Sea is likely delivered there from the Pacific Ocean. The maximum abundance of UCYN-A2 in the Chukchi Sea (2.9 × 10^3 copies L^{-1}) was about 40-fold lower than that in the Bering Sea (Shiozaki et al. 2017). UCYN-A abundance is known to be related to water temperature (Moisander et al. 2010), suggesting that UCYN-A2 abundance decreased with decreasing water temperature during their northward transit from the Bering Sea to the Chukchi Sea.

Nitrogen fixation and its importance in nitrogen cycle in the Chukchi Sea

We found that the vertical distribution pattern of the nitrogen fixation rate was complex, displaying sporadic subsurface peaks. In general, in tropical and subtropical waters, nitrogen fixation is high near the surface and decreases with depth. This can be explained by the prevalence of cyanobacterial diazotrophs that require light as an energy source (Church et al. 2009; Shiozaki et al. 2017). The complex vertical pattern of nitrogen fixation rates observed in this study could be due to the contribution of non-photosynthetic bacteria, whose nitrogen fixation is independent of the light environment, to nitrogen fixation. Interestingly, Cluster III phylotypes were dominant in our study area. As discussed in the previous section, these diazotrophs are putative anaerobes (Zehr et al. 2003) and were conceivably derived from coastal regions or sediments to the oxic water column. Anaerobes can be metabolically active in oxic seawater if they inhabit particles with anoxic microzones (Paerl and Prufert 1987). However, we lack evidence supporting (or refuting) the idea that Cluster III diazotrophs were fixing nitrogen in anoxic microzones. Whether the dominant Cluster III phylotypes contribute significantly to nitrogen fixation in oxic water columns clearly deserves further scrutiny.

Nitrogen fixation is regulated not only by light but also by other factors including iron, phosphorus, and temperature (Sohm et al. 2011 and references therein). The nitrogen fixation rate from the surface to the 0.1% light depth in the Chukchi Sea (0.08–3.60 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}) was higher than that reported in the literature for offshore stations (surface and SCM) in the Canadian sector of the Arctic Ocean (0.01–0.18 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}, Blais et al. 2012) (difference of means, \( p < 0.05 \), \( t \)-test), while it was comparable to that reported for estuarine stations (0.40–3.38 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}, Blais et al. 2012). Blais et al. (2012) suggested that the difference in nitrogen fixation between offshore and estuarine stations was attributable to the dissolved iron concentration. The nitrogen fixation enzyme nitrogenase contains iron in its active site, and thus, diazotrophs require much more iron for growth than other microbes (Kustka et al. 2002). Dissolved iron concentrations in the Chukchi Sea are very high (maximum, 33.1 nM) due to supply from shelf sediments and the Mackenzie River (Cid et al. 2012; Hioki et al. 2014; Kondo et al. 2016). Thus, the iron levels would be sufficient to support diazotrophs in our study area. Meanwhile, these nitrogen fixation rates are lower than those reported in lower latitude coastal environments, where the maximum nitrogen fixation often exceeds 10 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1} (Shiozaki et al. 2010, 2014b). Phosphorus limitation of nitrogen fixation generally occurs in phosphate-depleted waters (Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al. 2001). Phosphate was detected at all of the stations in our study area, and thus, did not appear to limit nitrogen fixation. There is a strong temperature difference between the Arctic and subtropical oceans. However, very high nitrogen fixation (> 60 nmol N L^{-1} d^{-1}) has been reported in a cold (4.1°C) temperate coastal environments (Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015), suggesting that temperature is not the reason for lower nitrogen fixation in the Chukchi Sea and Canadian Arctic coastal regions. Note that diazotroph community structure in our study area was notably different from that in other regions where Cluster I diazotrophs dominate (Farnelid et al. 2011; Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015), which may be related to the difference of nitrogen fixation activity.

The nitrate and ammonium assimilation rate was higher near the surface and decreased with depth, which is consistent with previous results for the Chukchi Sea (Lee et al. 2007; Nishino et al. 2011). Nitrate and ammonium assimilation integrated to the 0.1% light depth was within the range of previous studies in the Chukchi Sea (0.032–17.1 mmol and 1.02–36.9 N m^{-2} d^{-1}, respectively; Lee et al. 2007; Yun et al. 2014; Shiozaki et al. 2016). Our estimates showed that
pages.11:
nitrogen fixation accounts for at most only 1.00% of the total nitrogen assimilation rates (nitrogen fixation + nitrate and ammonium assimilation). In the Arctic Ocean, the assimilation of other forms of nitrogen (urea and amino acid) is reportedly as high as nitrate and ammonium assimilation (Baer et al. 2017). Therefore, nitrogen fixation is a minor process in the overall nitrogen cycle. However, nitrate assimilation in the off-shelf region was significantly lower than on the shelf, and nitrogen fixation in the off-shelf region sometimes exceeded nitrate assimilation and accounted for up to 17.0% of the sum of nitrate assimilation and nitrogen fixation in the euphotic zone, indicating a significant contribution to the local nitrogen cycle. Water stratification in the Arctic Ocean is preceded by ice melt, particularly in the Canada Basin, which includes the off-shelf region of the Chukchi Sea (McLaughlin and Carmack 2010; Nishino et al. 2011). Thus, nitrogen fixation could become more important to the nitrogen cycle of this region in the future.

Conclusions

This study documented that nitrogen fixation occurs throughout the Chukchi Sea, and has a local impact on the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen fixation was not affected by light or nitrate concentration, which could be due to the contribution of non-photosynthetic bacteria. Light-independent nitrogen fixation suggests the occurrence of nitrogen fixation below the euphotic zone and during the winter dark period. To the best of our knowledge, the western Arctic Ocean is the only oceanic region where Cluster III phyotypes dominate the diazotroph community in the euphotic zone. Arctic surface water masses can be broadly divided into waters originating in the Pacific and the Atlantic (Gordienko 1958). This water circulation pattern may differentiate the diazotroph community between the Chukchi Sea and Atlantic Arctic Ocean. We found that UCYN-A1 and -A2 in the Chukchi Sea were delivered from the Pacific Ocean. The Pacific inflow has tended to increase recently, inducing an increase in the heat flux (Woodgate et al. 2012; Itoh et al. 2013). This environmental change may alter the diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea.

Nitrogen fixation
Samples for nitrogen fixation were collected in duplicate acid-cleaned 1.2 L polycarbonate bottles. Nitrogen fixation was determined using the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas dissolution method (Mohr et al. 2010). Samples (1.2 L) collected for determining the initial \( ^{15} \)N enrichment of particulate organic matter were filtered immediately at the beginning of incubation (\( n = 1 \)). \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\)-enriched filtered seawater (50 mL) was injected, and the bottles were sealed with a thermoplastic elastomer cap. \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas was dissolved at a ratio of 10 mL \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) per 1 L seawater. The volume of dissolved N\(_2\) was calculated using the equation given by Weiss (1970), and we assumed that added \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) was completely dissolved. The resulting N\(_2\) substrate enrichment at the beginning of incubation was approximately 3–4% (Supporting Information Table S3). A recent study showed that commercial \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas could be contaminated by \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate and ammonium (Dabundo et al. 2014). Dabundo et al. (2014) suggested that the contamination may occur during the production process of the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas, and it differed among different batches, even for those from the same distributor, although they did not examine the product of SI Science (Yokohama, Japan). The SI Science \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas is produced by the oxidation of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium sulfate by potassium hypobromite (Nakane 1963), followed by purification using a molecular sieve and liquid nitrogen. Shiozaki et al. (2015b) examined the contamination of nitrate and ammonium for two different batches of the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas stock purchased from SI Science and found that the contamination was negligible (< nmol L\(^{-1}\)) for all batches examined. Furthermore, they reported that the contamination of nitrate and ammonium in a \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) dissolved water (10 mL \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) per 1 L seawater) was undetectable (< nmol L\(^{-1}\) level). In the present study, we added 50 mL of \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) dissolved water to the samples. Therefore, \( ^{15} \)N-labeled substrates in the samples were below 5 \( \times \) 10\(^{-2}\) nmol N L\(^{-1}\). When the substrate concentration in the seawater was 0.05 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) (the detection limit of our analysis), the concentration of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled substrate would be < 1/1000 lower than that of seawater. In this case, the \( ^{15} \)N concentration would be too low to detect the uptake rate (Shiozaki et al. 2009). Therefore, we believe that our estimates of the N\(_2\)-fixation rate were affected little by impurities in the \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) gas. The bottles were incubated in an on-deck incubator filled with flowing surface seawater for 24 h. Incubations were terminated by gentle filtration onto pre-combusted (450°C for 6 h) GF/F filters (Whatman). The filters were kept frozen before onshore analysis. The filters were dried at 50°C overnight, and then exposed to HCl fumes for 2 h. Total nitrogen and isotope ratios were determined using a DELTA V advantage mass spectrometer (Thermo Electron, Waltham, Massachusetts, U.S.A.) connected to a Flash EA elemental analyzer (Thermo Electron). The nitrogen fixation rate was calculated using the equation proposed by Montoya et al. (1996). We performed a sensitivity analysis for the nitrogen fixation measurements to determine quantifiable nitrogen fixation rates (Montoya et al. 1996; Gradoville et al. 2017). The minimum quantifiable rate for each sample was calculated using standard propagation of errors based on the observed variability between replicate samples, and ranged from 0.05 nmol N L\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\) to 3.30 nmol N L\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Supporting Information Table S3).

Nitrate and ammonium assimilation
Samples for nitrate assimilation were collected at all stations, and those for ammonium assimilation were collected at Sta. 32, 39, 47, 53, 54, 55, 56, 62, 68, 75, 82, 85, 94, 98, and 108. These samples were collected in acid-cleaned 1.2-L polycarbonate bottles during the daytime. Samples were also collected for nighttime incubation of ammonium assimilation. For nighttime incubation, the bottles were incubated without \( ^{15} \)N tracer in an on-deck incubator until midnight, and then \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium was added. For daytime incubation, \( ^{15} \)N tracer was added immediately after water collection. The nitrate and ammonium assimilation rates were determined by the Michaelis–Menten kinetics approach (Shiozaki et al. 2009) using samples obtained from the surface and 10% light depth. \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate (99 atom% \( ^{15} \)N; SI Science) was added at final tracer concentrations of 10 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 20 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 100 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and 2000 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and \( ^{15} \)N-labeled ammonium (99 atom% \( ^{15} \)N; SI Science) was added at final tracer concentrations of 8 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 25 nmol L\(^{-1}\), 125 nmol L\(^{-1}\), and 1250 nmol L\(^{-1}\). The enrichment of \( ^{15} \)N-labeled nitrate and ammonium in samples obtained from the 1% and 0.1% light depths averaged 23.3% ± 24.9% and 18.6% ± 13.7%, respectively, which was higher than the tracer level (< 10%). Discussion
Diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea
This study is the first to elucidate the diazotroph community structure in the Arctic Ocean using a deep sequencing approach. Although some studies have examined diazotroph communities in Arctic regions (Blais et al. 2012; Díez et al. 2012; Fernández-Méndez et al. 2016), these studies analyzed clone libraries with a limited number of sequences, being compromised by phylogenetic resolution. A notable finding of the present study is that Cluster III phylotypes dominated the diazotroph community in the Chukchi Sea. We found that Cluster III accounted for > 80% of the total nifH sequences examined, except for one surface sample. Cluster III includes putative anaerobes belonging to Bacteria and Archaea (Zehr et al. 2003) and has been reported to be a major constituent of the nifH sequences retrieved from marine and estuarine sediments (Bertics et al. 2013; Newell et al. 2016). Studies have also recovered Cluster III nifH sequences from coastal marine waters (e.g., Moisander et al. 2008; Bentzon-Tilia et al. 2015; Shiozaki et al. 2015a). In the Canadian Arctic, Blais et al. (2012) found many nifH sequences affiliated with Cluster III in water samples collected from rivers, estuaries, and fjords. By contrast, in offshore areas of the Arctic Ocean, the retrieved nifH sequences were mainly affiliated with Cluster I phylotypes including cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria (Díez et al. 2012; Fernández-Méndez et al. 2016). Considering this information, we speculate that Cluster III phylotypes in the investigated waters were allochthonous and derived from the coastal region or sediments.
